chem_ocrb.7.2.summary: Mastering PAG5 and PAG6 requires precise experimental technique, accurate colour change recognition, and rigorous volumetric calculations. You must know exact tests for cations, anions, and gases, alongside step-by-step procedures for acid-base titrations using phenolphthalein or methyl orange indicators. Examiners expect exact descriptions of observations, balanced ionic equations, and flawless mole calculations with correct units.

core.p: Practical Activity Group 5 (PAG5) covers the identification of chemical species through qualitative analysis tests, including flame tests, precipitation reactions, and gas tests. Practical Activity Group 6 (PAG6) covers quantitative analysis via acid-base titrations to find unknown concentrations. Both practicals demand high precision, cleanliness, and the exact use of analytical reagents to secure full marks in exams.
bullets: PAG5 uses chemical tests to identify specific ions and gases in unknown solutions or solids.
PAG6 determines exact reacting volumes through neutralisation reactions using burettes and pipettes.
Both practicals test your ability to make valid, reproducible observations and accurate numerical measurements.
Safety precautions such as wearing eye protection and handling concentrated acids with care are mandatory.

callouts.p: You can be asked about any part of PAG5 and PAG6 in Paper 1, 2, 3, or 4, including apparatus selection and safety.

core.p: Flame tests are used to identify metal ions (cations) present in solid compounds. The colour emitted when a sample is heated in a luminous blue Bunsen flame is characteristic of the metal ion. You must describe the exact colour produced without confusing similar shades like brick-red and lilac.
bullets: Dip a clean nichrome or platinum wire loop into concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl) to clean it, then into the solid sample.
Hold the wire loop in the edge of a roaring (blue) Bunsen burner flame.
Lithium ions (Li+) produce a crimson-red flame.
Sodium ions (Na+) produce a yellow-orange flame.
Potassium ions (K+) produce a lilac flame.
Calcium ions (Ca2+) produce an orange-red flame.
Copper(II) ions (Cu2+) produce a green flame.

callouts.p: Always clean the wire loop with concentrated acid and a roaring flame between tests to prevent cross-contamination.

core.p: Many metal cations form insoluble coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added. These precipitation reactions allow you to distinguish between transition metal ions and group 2/other metal ions based on precipitate colour and solubility in excess sodium hydroxide.
bullets: Copper(II) (Cu2+) forms a blue precipitate.
Iron(II) (Fe2+) forms a green precipitate that turns brown on standing in air due to oxidation.
Iron(III) (Fe3+) forms a brown precipitate.
Aluminium (Al3+), Calcium (Ca2+), and Magnesium (Mg2+) all form white precipitates with sodium hydroxide.
Aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide to form a colourless solution.
Calcium and magnesium hydroxide precipitates remain insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide.

callouts.p: An insoluble solid formed by the reaction of two solutions in a precipitation reaction.

core.h: 4. Anion Tests: Carbonates, Halides, and Sulfates
core.p: Anions (negative ions) are identified using specific reagent tests that produce effervescence, precipitates, or distinct chemical changes. You must learn the exact reagents, observations, and ionic equations for each test.
bullets: Carbonate ions (CO3 2-): Add dilute acid (like HCl). Effervescence is seen, and the gas turns limewater cloudy (carbon dioxide produced).
Sulfate ions (SO4 2-): Add dilute hydrochloric acid followed by barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms.
Chloride ions (Cl-): Add dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution. A white precipitate of silver chloride forms.
Bromide ions (Br-): Add dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution. A cream precipitate of silver bromide forms.
Iodide ions (I-): Add dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution. A yellow precipitate of silver iodide forms.

callouts.p: Always add dilute hydrochloric acid before barium chloride to remove carbonate impurities that would also form a white precipitate.

core.p: Identifying gases produced in chemical reactions is a core requirement of PAG5. You must know the exact test and positive result for each common gas.
bullets: Hydrogen (H2): Hold a burning splint at the open end of the test tube. A squeaky pop sound is heard.
Oxygen (O2): Hold a glowing splint inside the test tube. The splint relights.
Carbon dioxide (CO2): Bubble the gas through limewater. The limewater turns milky or cloudy.
Chlorine (Cl2): Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas. The litmus paper is bleached white (it may turn red briefly first due to acidity).
Ammonia (NH3): Hold damp red litmus paper in the gas. The paper turns blue.

callouts.p: Litmus paper must be damp for chlorine and ammonia tests so the gas can dissolve and react with water to show its properties.

core.p: Titrations are quantitative volumetric experiments used to find the exact concentration of an acid or alkali. By reacting a known volume of one solution with an unknown solution using a suitable indicator, you can calculate the unknown concentration accurately.
bullets: Apparatus required: Burette, volumetric pipette, conical flask, pipette filler, and a white tile.
The burette measures variable volumes of liquid delivered with an accuracy of 0.05 cm3.
The volumetric pipette measures a fixed volume of liquid (e.g., 25.0 cm3) very accurately.
The conical flask holds the reaction mixture and is swirled during titration.
A white tile is placed under the conical flask to make colour changes easier to see.

callouts.p: A volumetric technique where a solution of known concentration is added from a burette to a known volume of another solution until neutralisation is complete.

core.p: Executing a titration with high precision requires careful preparation and technique. Examiners frequently test your understanding of the correct rinsing steps and operational procedures.
bullets: Rinse the burette with the acid solution to be put inside it.
Rinse the volumetric pipette with the alkali solution to be transferred.
Rinse the conical flask with distilled water only (rinsing with solutions would alter the moles of reactant).
Fill the burette below eye level, removing any air bubble at the tip, and record the initial burette reading to the nearest 0.05 cm3.
Use the pipette and pipette filler to transfer exactly 25.0 cm3 of alkali into the conical flask.
Add 2-3 drops of a suitable indicator to the conical flask.

callouts.t: Never Rinse Conical Flask with Reagents
callouts.p: Rinsing the conical flask with acid or alkali changes the number of moles inside it, ruining the titration result. Distilled water is fine.

core.p: Choosing the correct indicator is essential for a successful titration. The indicator must change colour sharply at the neutralisation point (equivalence point). Universal indicator is never used because its colour change is too gradual.
bullets: Phenolphthalein: Colourless in acid, pink/magenta in alkali. Used for strong acid-strong alkali and strong acid-weak alkali titrations.
Methyl orange: Red in acid, yellow in alkali (orange at end-point). Used for strong acid-strong alkali and weak acid-strong alkali titrations.
Add dropwise near the end-point when the colour begins to change.
Swirl the conical flask constantly to ensure complete mixing.

callouts.p: Learn the exact start and end colours for phenolphthalein and methyl orange for both acidic and alkaline conditions.

core.p: To ensure reliability, titrations must be repeated until concordant results are obtained. Calculations use moles, concentration, and volume to find unknown quantities.
bullets: Concordant results are titres that are within 0.1 cm3 of each other (rough titration is excluded from the mean).
Calculate the mean titre using only concordant results.
Formula: Moles = Concentration (mol/dm3) x Volume (dm3).
Concentration (g/dm3) = Concentration (mol/dm3) x Relative Formula Mass (Mr).
Always convert volumes from cm3 to dm3 by dividing by 1000.

callouts.p: Titration results that are very close to each other, typically within 0.1 cm3 of agreement.

core.p: Mastering titration calculations requires a structured 4-step approach: find moles of the known substance, use the stoichiometric ratio from the balanced equation, calculate moles of the unknown substance, and finally determine its concentration or volume.
bullets: Step 1: Calculate moles of the substance with known concentration (Moles = Concentration x Volume).
Step 2: Use the balancing numbers from the balanced chemical equation to find the molar ratio.
Step 3: Calculate the moles of the unknown substance using the ratio.
Step 4: Calculate the concentration or volume of the unknown solution (Concentration = Moles / Volume).

callouts.p: Always show every intermediate calculation step in exam questions to secure method marks even if your final arithmetic error is minor.

core.p: In addition to wet chemistry tests, modern analytical chemistry uses instrumental methods to identify ions and compounds quickly and accurately.
bullets: Instrumental methods are more accurate, sensitive, and rapid than traditional chemical tests, and can analyse very small sample sizes.
Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method used to identify metal ions in solution.
The sample is heated in a flame, and the light emitted passes through a spectroscope.
The output is a line spectrum that is unique to each metal ion, allowing identification even in mixtures.

callouts.p: An instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions by measuring the light emitted when heated.

core.p: Comparing traditional chemical tests with instrumental methods involves weighing advantages and disadvantages across cost, time, and accuracy.
bullets: Traditional wet chemistry tests (PAG5) are cheap and require simple equipment, but are qualitative and less sensitive.
Instrumental methods (like flame emission spectroscopy) are extremely sensitive, fast, and accurate, and can detect tiny traces of substances.
Disadvantages of instrumental methods include expensive equipment, requirement for trained operators, and calibration using reference standards.

callouts.p: Always remember: instrumental methods are faster, more sensitive, and more accurate than wet chemistry tests.

analogy.t: The Lock and Key of Chemical Analysis
analogy.p: Think of PAG5 ion testing like matching fingerprints to a suspect in a crime database: every ion produces a unique, unmistakable test result (colour, precipitate, or gas) just like a fingerprint matches a specific individual. For PAG6 titrations, think of baking a cake where adding exact amounts of ingredients is crucial; adding even one drop too much of an acid or alkali ruins the neutralisation balance, just like adding too much salt ruins a recipe. Where this analogy breaks down is that chemical reactions follow strict stoichiometric mole ratios rather than culinary proportions, and chemical tests can occasionally give false positives if interfering ions are present.

terms.d: A volumetric technique used to find the concentration of a solution by reacting it with another of known concentration.
A graduated glass tube with a tap used for delivering variable volumes of liquid accurately.
A volumetric glass tube used to measure a single fixed volume of liquid with high precision.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether it is in an acidic or alkaline solution.
Titration results that lie within 0.1 cm3 of each other.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react.
The point in a titration where the acid and alkali have completely reacted according to the stoichiometric equation.
A qualitative analytical test used to identify metal cations by the characteristic colour they emit in a flame.
An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide used to test for carbon dioxide gas.
An instrumental method used to identify metal ions by their characteristic line emission spectra.
The point in a titration where the indicator changes colour permanently.
The amount of solute dissolved in a specific volume of solvent, measured in mol/dm3 or g/dm3.
The reaction between an acid and a base producing a salt and water.

mistakes.w: Washing the conical flask with sodium hydroxide solution before titration.
mistakes.r: The conical flask must only be rinsed with distilled water; any reagent left inside alters the number of moles.

mistakes.w: Saying copper(II) forms a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide.
mistakes.r: Copper(II) forms a distinct blue precipitate.
Universal indicator has a gradual colour change; you must use phenolphthalein or methyl orange with a sharp end-point.

mistakes.w: Leaving an air bubble in the burette jet before starting a titration.
mistakes.r: The jet must be completely filled with liquid before taking the initial reading, otherwise the titre volume will be too high.

mistakes.w: Saying a glowing splint pops in hydrogen.
mistakes.r: A glowing splint relights in oxygen; hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a burning splint.

mistakes.w: Adding barium chloride without adding dilute acid first in the sulfate test.
mistakes.r: Dilute hydrochloric acid must be added first to remove carbonate ions that would also form a white precipitate.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert cm3 to dm3 when calculating moles.
mistakes.r: Always divide volume in cm3 by 1000 to convert to dm3.

mistakes.w: Stating flame tests identify non-metal anions.
mistakes.r: Flame tests are exclusively used to identify metal cations.

exam.q: Describe the test to identify sulfate ions in an unknown solution. Include the reagent and the positive observation.
model: Add dilute hydrochloric acid followed by barium chloride solution
exam.tip: Always mention adding dilute acid first to remove interfering ions.

exam.q: A student carries out a titration using sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid with phenolphthalein indicator. State the colour change at the end-point.
model: Turns colourless at the end-point when acid is added
exam.tip: State the starting and ending colours clearly.

exam.q: Explain why the volumetric pipette is rinsed with the solution it will contain, but the conical flask is rinsed only with distilled water.
model: Pipette is rinsed with solution to remove water traces that would dilute the solution and alter the measured volume
Conical flask is rinsed with distilled water because water does not change the number of moles of reactant inside the flask
exam.tip: Focus on how water affects the number of moles of reactant.

exam.q: Give the test and positive result for chlorine gas.
model: Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas
The litmus paper is bleached white
exam.tip: Litmus paper must be damp for the test to work.

exam.q: Calculate the concentration of hydrochloric acid in mol/dm3 if 25.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol/dm3 sodium hydroxide is neutralized by 20.0 cm3 of the acid.
model: Moles of NaOH = 0.025 dm3 x 0.100 mol/dm3 = 0.0025 mol
Concentration of HCl = 0.0025 mol / 0.020 dm3 = 0.125 mol/dm3
exam.tip: Show every step clearly and include units in the final answer.

exam.q: State the flame test colour for potassium ions.
exam.tip: Learn flame test colours precisely; do not confuse lilac with crimson or orange-red.

exam.q: Explain why concordant titres are obtained in a titration.
model: To allow calculation of an accurate mean titre by discarding anomalous results
exam.tip: Mention both reliability and discarding anomalies.

exam.q: A solid unknown compound gives a green flame in a flame test and forms a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide. Identify the metal cation.
exam.tip: Combine evidence from both tests to deduce the ion.

exam.q: Describe how to test for carbon dioxide gas and state the positive observation.
exam.tip: Specify limewater and the milky observation.

exam.q: Give two advantages of instrumental analysis methods compared to traditional chemical tests.
model: Any two from: more accurate, faster, more sensitive, uses smaller sample sizes
exam.tip: Instrumental methods are superior in speed and sensitivity.

worked.q: Calculate the concentration of sulfuric acid in g/dm3 if 25.0 cm3 of 0.200 mol/dm3 sodium hydroxide is neutralized by 12.5 cm3 of sulfuric acid. (H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O, Mr of H2SO4 = 98)
steps: Step 1: Calculate moles of NaOH used (Moles = Concentration x Volume in dm3). Moles = 0.0250 x 0.200 = 0.00500 mol.
Step 2: Use the balanced equation (1 H2SO4 reacts with 2 NaOH) to find moles of sulfuric acid. Moles of H2SO4 = 0.00500 / 2 = 0.00250 mol.
Step 3: Calculate concentration in mol/dm3 (Concentration = Moles / Volume in dm3). Conc = 0.00250 / 0.0125 = 0.200 mol/dm3.
Step 4: Convert concentration to g/dm3 by multiplying by Mr (98). Concentration in g/dm3 = 0.200 x 98 = 19.6 g/dm3.

worked.q: A student titrates 25.0 cm3 of sodium carbonate solution with 0.150 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid. The mean titre is 20.50 cm3. Calculate the concentration of the sodium carbonate solution in mol/dm3. (Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2)
steps: Step 1: Calculate moles of HCl added (Moles = 0.02050 dm3 x 0.150 mol/dm3 = 0.003075 mol).
Step 2: Use the stoichiometric ratio from the balanced equation (1 Na2CO3 : 2 HCl). Moles of Na2CO3 = 0.003075 / 2 = 0.0015375 mol.
Step 3: Calculate the concentration of sodium carbonate (Concentration = Moles / Volume in dm3). Conc = 0.0015375 / 0.0250 = 0.0615 mol/dm3.
